answer: Departure-window spacing.** Each identity gets a slot to launch its first voyage; the slot is assigned by hashing its address into a shared clock, and only one departure is allowed per window. A burst of new identities must either wait many windows (delaying the attack by hours or days) or spread across windows, which exposes the cluster's traffic shape to rate detection. The harbor admits identities on this schedule, so the ocean of pending arrivals is visible and capped. Each attacker identity costs the full window wait plus slot occupancy, making mass creation slow and detectable.
